cards.question: What does @Transactional do?
cards.answer: It runs the method inside one database transaction. Everything is committed together when the method returns, or rolled back together if it throws an exception.

cards.question: What is dirty checking in Hibernate?
cards.answer: Inside a transaction, Hibernate keeps a snapshot of every entity it loaded. At commit it compares each entity with its snapshot and sends an UPDATE for the ones that changed, without any save() call.

cards.question: Why can't a JPA entity be a Java record?
cards.answer: Hibernate creates an entity with a no-argument constructor and then fills its fields one by one. A record has no empty constructor and its fields are final.

cards.question: What does FetchType.LAZY mean on a @ManyToOne field?
cards.answer: The related entity is not loaded together with the owner. Hibernate puts a proxy in its place and loads the real data the first time one of its fields is read, which must happen inside a transaction.

cards.question: Why should a REST controller return a DTO instead of the entity?
cards.answer: You decide exactly which fields leave the server, the API stays stable when the table changes, and you avoid lazy-loading errors and endless loops when Jackson serializes relationships.

cards.question: What does @Valid on a @RequestBody parameter do?
cards.answer: Spring runs the Bean Validation annotations of the request object before the controller method. If a rule fails, Spring throws MethodArgumentNotValidException and the method never runs.

cards.question: @NotNull, @NotEmpty or @NotBlank: which one rejects "   "?
cards.answer: Only @NotBlank. @NotNull accepts any text that is not null, and @NotEmpty accepts text with at least one character, even if it is only spaces.

cards.question: What does spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto=update do, and what can it not do?
cards.answer: At startup Hibernate creates missing tables and columns from the entities. It never renames, removes or repairs columns, which is why real projects use a migration tool such as Flyway.

cards.question: How does Spring Data turn findByDeckIdOrderByIdAsc into SQL?
cards.answer: It reads the method name: findBy starts the WHERE clause, DeckId means deck.id, and OrderByIdAsc becomes ORDER BY id ASC. A misspelled field name makes the application fail at startup.

cards.question: What is a foreign key constraint?
cards.answer: A rule kept by the database itself: a column such as card.deck_id may only contain the id of a row that exists in the referenced table. Inserts and deletes that would break it are refused.

cards.question: What is the difference between == and ===?
cards.answer: === compares value and type without converting anything. == converts the values first, so "2" == 2 is true while "2" === 2 is false. Use ===.

cards.question: What do you get when you read a property that does not exist, such as error.messsage?
cards.answer: undefined. JavaScript raises no error, so a misspelled name only shows up later, for example as an empty text or the word undefined on the page.

cards.question: Why does fetch need two awaits?
cards.answer: The first await waits for the response headers and gives a Response object. The second, await response.json(), waits for the body to arrive and be parsed.

cards.question: Does fetch reject on a 404 or 500 response?
cards.answer: No. fetch only rejects when the request cannot be made at all, for example on a network failure. You have to check response.ok yourself.

cards.question: What is a closure?
cards.answer: A function that keeps access to the variables of the place where it was created, even after that outer function has returned.

cards.question: What is event delegation?
cards.answer: One listener on a parent element handles the events of all its children, because events bubble up. event.target.closest(selector) finds which child was clicked, and it keeps working for elements added later.

cards.question: What does event.preventDefault() do?
cards.answer: It stops the browser's default action for that event, for example a form submit reloading the page or the Space key scrolling it.

cards.question: What does ?? do, and how is it different from ||?
cards.answer: a ?? b gives b only when a is null or undefined. a || b gives b for every falsy value, including 0 and the empty string.

cards.question: Why does array.sort() surprise people?
cards.answer: It changes the original array, and without a comparator it compares the values as text, so [10, 9, 1].sort() gives [1, 10, 9].

cards.question: What does const prevent, and what does it not prevent?
cards.answer: It prevents assigning a new value to the variable. It does not make an object or an array unchangeable: its contents can still be modified.

cards.question: What does git add do?
cards.answer: It puts changes into the staging area: the set of changes that the next commit will record.

cards.question: When is git commit --amend safe to use?
cards.answer: Only before the commit has been pushed. It replaces the last commit with a new one, so changing a commit that is already on the remote would need a force push.

cards.question: What does git push --force-with-lease protect you from?
cards.answer: It replaces the remote branch only if the remote still points where you last saw it, so it never overwrites commits that someone else pushed in the meantime.

cards.question: What does git push -u do?
cards.answer: It pushes the branch and links it to the remote branch, so later pushes and pulls on that branch need no extra arguments.

cards.question: What is the difference between git branch -d and git branch -D?
cards.answer: -d deletes a branch only if it is already merged. -D deletes it even if it contains work that was never merged.

cards.question: What is a sprint?
cards.answer: A fixed time box, usually one or two weeks, in which the team delivers a chosen set of backlog items toward a sprint goal.

cards.question: What is velocity?
cards.answer: The number of story points a team actually finishes in a sprint. Only items that are fully done count.

cards.question: Why are story points not hours?
cards.answer: They measure relative size, a mix of effort, complexity and uncertainty. People compare sizes much more reliably than they guess hours.

cards.question: What is the Definition of Done?
cards.answer: One checklist that every item must pass before it counts as done, so done means the same thing every time.

cards.question: What is the difference between a sprint review and a retrospective?
cards.answer: The review inspects the product: what was built, against the sprint goal. The retrospective inspects the process: how the team worked and what to improve.
